Indeed, through His defense of them they gain victory over their enemy, and were it not for His defense of them, their enemy would snatch them away and annihilate them.

This defense of them is in proportion to their faith and according to its measure. If faith is strong, the defense is strong. Whoever finds good, let him praise Allah, and whoever finds otherwise, let him blame no one but himself.

[Section: On the levels of the jihad against Satan]

As for the jihad against Satan, it has two levels. The first: striving to repel the doubts and suspicions that he casts upon the servant, which undermine faith. The second: striving to repel the corrupt wills and desires that he casts into him. The first jihad is followed by certainty (yaqin), and the second is followed by patience (sabr). The Exalted said: ﴿And We made among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient and were certain of Our signs﴾ [as-Sajdah: 24].

He informed that leadership in religion is attained only through patience and certainty. Patience repels the desires and corrupt wills, and certainty repels doubts and suspicions.

[Section: On the levels of the jihad against the disbelievers and hypocrites]

As for the jihad against the disbelievers and hypocrites, it has four levels: with the heart, the tongue, wealth, and the self. The jihad against the disbelievers is especially by the hand, and the jihad against the hypocrites is especially by the tongue.

[Section: On the jihad against the lords of injustice, innovation, and wrongdoing]

As for the jihad against the lords of injustice, innovation, and evil deeds, it has three levels. The first: by the hand, if able. If he is unable, he moves to the tongue. If he is unable, he strives with his heart. These are thirteen levels of jihad. And "Whoever dies without having fought, nor having spoken of fighting in his soul, dies upon a branch of hypocrisy."

[Section: On the conditions of jihad]

Jihad is not complete except with migration (hijrah), and neither migration nor jihad is complete except with faith. Those who hope for the mercy of Allah are those who uphold these three. The Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated and striven in the way of Allah—those hope for the mercy of Allah, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 218].

Just as faith is obligatory upon every person, two migrations are obligatory upon him at all times: a migration to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, through monotheism, sincerity, turning back (inabah), reliance (tawakkul), fear, hope, love, and repentance; and a migration to His Messenger through following him, submitting to his command, affirming his report, and giving precedence to his command and report over the command and report of others. «Whoever's migration was to Allah and His Messenger, his migration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever's migration was for worldly gain he might obtain, or for a woman he might marry, his migration is to what he migrated for.» He also obligated upon him the striving against his own self for the sake of Allah, and the striving against his Satan. All of this is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) for which no one can substitute for another.

As for the jihad against the disbelievers and hypocrites, it may be sufficient for some of the Ummah to undertake it once the objective of jihad is achieved by them.

((Part Seven))

(Section)

Beware of lying, for it corrupts your perception of things as they actually are, and it corrupts your conveying of them to people. The liar makes the non-existent appear existent and the existent appear non-existent, the truth appear false and the false appear true, the good appear evil and the evil appear good. His perception and knowledge are thereby corrupted as a punishment for him. Then he impresses that same picture upon the listener who is deceived by him and relies on him, so the listener's perception and knowledge are corrupted too. The liar's soul turns away from the reality that exists, inclines toward non-existence, and prefers falsehood. When the faculty of his perception and knowledge, which is the origin of every voluntary act, becomes corrupted, those acts are corrupted as well, and the effect of lying spreads into them. Their proceeding from him becomes like the proceeding of lies from the tongue. He therefore gains no benefit from his tongue or from his deeds. For this reason lying is the foundation of wickedness, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Lying leads to wickedness, and wickedness leads to the Fire."

Lying first spreads from the soul to the tongue and corrupts it, then it spreads to the limbs (jawarih) and corrupts their actions, just as it corrupted the tongue's speech. So lying encompasses his sayings, his deeds and his states, and corruption becomes firmly established in him. His disease spreads toward ruin unless God reaches him with the remedy of truthfulness, which uproots all of this from its root. For this reason the root of all the deeds of the heart is truthfulness, and its opposites, such as ostentation (riya'), self-admiration ('ujb), arrogance (kibr), boasting (fakhr), conceit (khuyala'), insolence (batar), wantonness (ashar), incapacity ('ajz), laziness (kasal), cowardice (jubn), and humiliation (mahana), and others, have lying as their root. Every good deed, outward or inward, originates in truthfulness, and every corrupt deed, outward or inward, originates in lying. God, exalted is He, punishes the liar by causing him to be sluggish, holding him back and hindering him from his interests and benefits, and He rewards the truthful by enabling him to attend to the interests of his worldly life and his Hereafter. The interests of this world and the Hereafter are not drawn in by anything like truthfulness, nor are their corruptions and harms produced by anything like lying. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, fear God and be with the truthful.﴾ And He said: ﴿This is a day on which the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness.﴾ And He said: ﴿But when the matter is resolved, it would have been better for them if they had been truthful with God.﴾ And He said: ﴿And those who gave excuses among the bedouins came to be permitted [to stay behind], and those who lied to God and His Messenger sat [at home]. There will strike those who disbelieved among them a painful punishment.﴾

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 9, verse 92:

They were not praised for the sorrow itself; rather, they were praised for what that sorrow indicated of the strength of their faith, in that they stayed behind from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) because they were unable to spend (for the expedition). In this there is an allusion (ta'ridh) to the hypocrites, who did not grieve over their staying behind, but rather envied themselves for it.

(A Striking Benefit)

It is not permissible to omit the conjunction (harf al-'atf) by elision (idmar), contrary to al-Farisi and those who followed him, because particles are indicators of meanings within the speaker's mind. If they were elided, the listener would need a revelation to disclose what is in the mind of the one addressing him. The ruling on conjunctions in this matter is the same as the ruling on particles of negation, emphasis, hope, wish, and others. The exception is that interrogative particles may, in some contexts, permissibly be elided, because the questioner has a bearing different from that of the one who informs; but this is rare.

If it is said: How then do you treat the words of the poet:

"How did you wake, how did you spend the evening, by what / means the affection is established in the heart of the noble one"

Is this not an elision of the conjunction, the original being "How did you wake and how did you spend the evening"? It is said: It is not so, and the conjunction is not intended here at all. Were it intended, the purpose the poet aimed at would be undermined, because he did not mean that affection is confined to these two words without constancy upon them; rather, he meant that the repetition of these two words constantly establishes affection. Had the wa' been present, the establishment of affection would have been confined to these two words without constancy or continuity upon them, and the poet did not intend that. He intended to make the opening of the speech a heading for the whole topic, meaning continuation in this speech and persistence in it, just as you say: "I read alif-ba' (alif, ba'), gathering these letters as a heading for the whole chapter and a title for the intended aim." Had you said "I read alif and ba'," you would have implied the completion of what was read, since you conjoined the ba' to the alif and not to what follows, so the implied meaning of the discourse would be that you had read only these two letters. Better than this is to say: the insertion of the wa' here corrupts the meaning, because the intent is that this word alone establishes affection, and that this word alone establishes it according to the occurrence of the meeting; whichever of them finds its requirement and is persisted in establishes affection. Had the wa' been inserted, affection would be established only by the two words together. A parallel to this is your saying, "Feed so-and-so something," and he says, "What should I feed him?" and you say, "Feed him dates, curds, raisins, meat": you did not intend the gathering of all of these, but you meant "feed him one of these, whichever is easy." From this is the authentic hadith, traced to the Prophet: "A man gave in charity from his dinar, from his dirham, from a measure (sa') of his wheat" (narrated by Muslim, al-Nasa'i and Ahmad). And from it is the saying of 'Umar: "A man prayed in a waistwrap (izar) and a cloak (rida'), in trousers (sarawil) and a cloak, in breeches (tiban) and a cloak." In all of this the omission of the conjunction is required, and the intent is not gathering.

If it is said: What do you say about the expression "hit Zayd, 'Amr, Khalid": is not the wa' elided here? It is said: It is not so, for if the wa' were implied, the command would be restricted to those named and would not extend beyond them; rather, the intent is to indicate by them others besides them. From this is the saying, "I arranged the book chapter by chapter (baban babaan)," and "I divided the money dirham by dirham." It is not an elision of the conjunction; had it been so, the matter would be confined to two dirhams and two chapters.

As for what they cited from the words of the Exalted: ﴿Nor [is there blame] upon those who came to you that you might mount them; you said, "I cannot find that upon which I can mount you"﴾

What led them to this is that the response (jawab) of "idha" is His words: ﴿They turned back while their eyes overflowed with tears﴾, and you did not have anything to mount them on, so they turned back weeping; hence the wa' in "qulta" is supposed to be implied, since it is conjoined to the conditional verb, which is "ataw-ka." This is the statement of their argument, and there is no proof in it, because the response of "idha" in His saying "qulta la ajidu" is what is meant; the meaning is: when they came to you that you might mount them, you did not have anything to mount them on, so He expressed this by His saying "you said, 'I cannot find that upon which I can mount you,'" for a striking subtlety: an indication of their confirmation of him, and that they were content, in their knowledge of the impossibility, with the mere report he gave them by his saying: ﴿I cannot find that upon which I can mount you﴾. This differs from saying "they did not find with you that upon which to mount them," for that would make the explanation of their grief separate from his report. Likewise, had it been said "you did not find that upon which to mount them," this would not convey the meaning. So reflect on it, for it is striking.

If it is said: With what does His saying ﴿they turned back while their eyes overflowed﴾ connect, since it is a conjunction to what precedes it, for it is not a new sentence?

The answer: the omission of the conjunction here is from the striking features of speech, because of the intensity of its connection to what precedes it and its occurrence in the position of explanation, so that it is, as it were, that itself.

**Section: [The Happy Followers]**

As for the happy followers, they are of two kinds.

The first kind have the status of independent standing. Concerning them Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them with good conduct, Allah is well pleased with them, and they are well pleased with Him.﴾

These are the happy ones for whom Allah's good pleasure is established. They are the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and everyone who follows them with good conduct until the Day of Resurrection.

This is not restricted to the generation that saw them alone. The Successors (al-tabi'un) were specified as those who had seen the Companions only by customary usage, so that they could be distinguished from those after them. It is said: "The Successors" applies absolutely only to that generation. Otherwise, everyone who treads their path is among the Successors who follow them with good conduct, and is among those with whom Allah is well pleased and who are well pleased with Him.

Allah, glorified is He, qualified this following by making it a following "with good conduct," not an absolute following. It is not achieved merely by intention, or by following in one matter while opposing in another. Rather, it is a following accompanied by good conduct. The particle الباء (al-ba', the "bi-") here is for accompaniment.

Good conduct and following are a condition for attaining Allah's good pleasure and His Gardens. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves, reciting to them His verses and purifying them and teaching them the Book and wisdom, although they had been before in clear error. And [He sent him] to others of them who have not yet joined them. And He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise. That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills, and Allah is the possessor of great bounty.﴾

The "first ones" (al-awwalun) are those who met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and accompanied him.

The "others" (al-akharun) are those who have not joined them, meaning everyone after them who follows their methodology until the Day of Resurrection. Their lateness and non-attainment is in virtue and rank; indeed, they are below them, so non-attainment is in rank.

The two statements are like mutually implying ones, for those after them cannot reach them either in virtue or in time. These two categories are the happy ones.

(Benefit)

Three of the Companions combined being both Helpers and Emigrants, as mentioned by Ibn Ishaq in his Sirah (biography of the Prophet):

- One of them is Dhakwan ibn Abd Qays of the Banu al-Khazraj.
Ibn Ishaq said: "He went out to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in Makkah, then he emigrated from it to Madinah. He was called 'an Emigrant-Helper.' He witnessed Badr and was killed as a martyr at Uhud."

- And al-Abbas ibn Ubadah ibn Nadlah, also of the Banu al-Khazraj.
Ibn Ishaq said: "He was among those who went out to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in Makkah, and he remained with him there. He was killed as a martyr on the Day of Uhud."

- And Uqbah ibn Wahb. He went out to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Madinah to Makkah, and he was called "an Emigrant-Helper, an ally of the Banu al-Khazraj."

**[Section: Issuing Legal Verdicts Based on the Salaf's Reports and the Companions' Verdicts]**

**[Statement on the Permissibility of Issuing Verdicts Based on the Salaf's Reports]**

On the permissibility of issuing verdicts (fatwa) based on the reports of the early generations (al-athar al-salafiyyah) and the verdicts of the Companions; and that these are more worthy of being adopted than the opinions and verdicts of later scholars; and that their closeness to correctness is in proportion to the closeness of their people to the era of the Messenger, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him and his family; and that the verdicts of the Companions are more worthy of being adopted than the verdicts of the Successors, and the verdicts of the Successors are more worthy than those of the Successors' successors, and so on. Whenever the time of the Messenger is nearer, correctness is more prevalent. This is a judgment in terms of the category as a whole, not in terms of each individual question. Likewise, the era of the Successors, though superior to the era of their successors, is so in terms of the category, not in terms of every single person. However, those who are excelling in the earlier era are more numerous than those excelling in the later era. Similarly, correctness in their statements is more abundant than correctness in the statements of those after them. The disparity between the knowledge of the earlier and later scholars is like the disparity between them in virtue and religion.

Perhaps it is not permissible for the mufti (jurist issuing verdicts) or the judge before Allah to issue verdicts and judge by the statement of so-and-so among the later scholars, who are followers of the Imams (muqallidun, those who practice taqlid, i.e., following a school), adopting his opinion and preference, and to abandon issuing verdicts and judging by the statement of al-Bukhari, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Ali ibn al-Madini, Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazi, and their likes. Rather, he abandons the statements of Ibn al-Mubarak, al-Awza'i, Sufyan al-Thawri, Sufyan ibn Uyaynah, Hammad ibn Zayd, Hammad ibn Salamah, and their likes. Rather, he does not even give regard to the statements of Ibn Abi Dhi'b, al-Zuhri, and al-Layth ibn Sa'd, and their likes. Rather, he does not even count the statements of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan, al-Qasim, Salim, Ata', Tawus, Jabir ibn Zayd, Shurayh, Abu Wa'il, and Ja'far ibn Muhammad, and their kind, which are permissible to adopt. Rather, he considers the statements of the later followers of those who imitated him (taqlid) to take precedence over the verdicts of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Umar, Uthman, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu al-Darda', Zayd ibn Thabit, Abd Allah ibn Abbas, Abd Allah ibn Umar, Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, and their kind. Then he does not know what his excuse will be tomorrow before Allah, if he equates the statements and verdicts of those [later] with the statements and verdicts of these [Companions]. How much more so if he prefers them over these? How much more so if he specifies adopting them as a binding ruling and as a verdict, and prohibits adopting the statements of the Companions, and deems it permissible to punish whoever opposes the later scholars in this, and testifies against him with innovation, misguidance, and opposition to the people of knowledge, and that he is plotting against Islam? By Allah, he has taken the well-known proverb: "She accused me of her own ailment and slipped away." He has named the heirs of the Messenger by his own name, clothed them in his garments, and cast his own ailment upon them. Many of these people shout, cry out, say, and declare that all the Ummah must adopt the statement of the one whom we have imitated as our religion, and that it is not permissible to adopt the statements of Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali, and others among the Companions.

This is the statement of someone who adopted it and imitated it. May Allah grant him what he has chosen, and reward him on the Day of Resurrection with the fullest reward.

What we hold to be our religion before Allah is the opposite of this statement, and a refutation of it. So we say:

When a Companion makes a statement, either another Companion opposes him or does not oppose him. If one of his equals opposes him, the statement of neither one of them is a proof against the other. If someone more knowledgeable than him opposes him, as when the Rightly-Guided Caliphs, or some of them, oppose others among the Companions in a ruling, is the side in which the Rightly-Guided Caliphs, or some of them, stand a proof against the others? On this there are two statements among the scholars, and these are two narrations from Imam Ahmad. The correct view is that the side in which the Caliphs or some of them stand is preferred and more worthy of being adopted than the other side. If all four are on one side, there is no doubt that it is correct. If most of them are on one side, correctness is more likely there. If they are two against two, then the side of Abu Bakr and Umar is closer to correctness. If Abu Bakr and Umar disagree, then correctness is with Abu Bakr.

This is a general principle whose details are known only to one who has experience and familiarity with what the Companions disagreed about and with the stronger of their statements. It is sufficient in this to know the preferability of al-Siddiq's statement on the grandfather and the siblings, and that a triple divorce pronounced with one utterance counts as one time only, even if the three are pronounced, and on the permissibility of selling umm al-walad (slave-mothers who have borne a master's child). When a fair-minded scholar examines the evidences for these issues from both sides, it becomes clear to him that the side of al-Siddiq is stronger. Some of that has already been mentioned in the issue of the grandfather and the triple divorce with one utterance.

No single explicit text opposing al-Siddiq is ever preserved from him, and no verdict or ruling of his whose basis is weak is ever preserved. This is a confirmation that his caliphate was a caliphate of prophethood.

**[Section: Al-Shafi'i's Opinion on the Statements of the Companions]**

If a Companion does not oppose another Companion, then either his statement is widely known among the Companions or it is not. If it is widely known, then what the majority of the groups of jurists hold is that it is a consensus (ijma') and a proof. A group among them said it is a proof but not a consensus. A small group of the theologians (mutakallimun) and some later jurists said it is neither a consensus nor a proof.

If his statement is not widely known, or it is not known whether it was widely known or not, then people differ on whether it is a proof or not. What the majority of the Ummah hold is that it is a proof. This is the statement of the majority of the Hanafis. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan stated it explicitly and mentioned a text from Abu Hanifah. It is also the position of Malik and his companions, and his conduct in his Muwatta' is evidence for it. It is the statement of Ishaq ibn Rahawayh and Abu Ubayd. It is the explicit position of Imam Ahmad on several occasions, and the choice of the majority of his companions. It is also the explicit position of al-Shafi'i in the Qadim (old) and the Jadid (new) doctrines. As for the Qadim, his companions acknowledge it. As for the Jadid, many of them report from him that it is not a proof. In this report from him there is a very clear problem. For not a single letter is preserved from him in the Jadid that the statement of a Companion is not a proof. The most that they cling to in transmitting this is that he reports statements of Companions in the Jadid and then opposes them. If they were a proof for him, he would not have opposed them. But this is a very weak basis, since a mujtahid (independent jurist) opposing a specific evidence in favor of what he considers stronger does not indicate that he does not regard it as evidence in general. Rather, he opposed one evidence in favor of another that he considered stronger. Some have clung to the claim that in the Jadid, when he mentions the statements of the Companions, he agrees with them but does not rely on them alone as he does with texts. Rather, he supports them with various kinds of analogies (qiyas). Sometimes he mentions them and explicitly opposes them, and sometimes he agrees with them but does not rely on them, supporting them with another evidence instead. This is also a basis weaker than the previous one. For the convergence, mutual support, and reinforcement of evidences is a practice of the people of knowledge, past and present. Mentioning a second and third evidence does not indicate that what they mentioned before it is not evidence.

Al-Shafi'i explicitly stated in the Jadid, from the narration of al-Rabi' from him, that the statement of the Companions is a proof that must be followed. He said: "Newly introduced matters are of two kinds. One of them is what is newly introduced that opposes the Book, or the Sunnah, or consensus, or a report (athar). This is the misguided innovation." Al-Rabi' took this from him in Egypt. He made opposing a report which is neither a Book, nor a Sunnah, nor a consensus a misguidance. This is above being merely a proof.

Al-Bayhaqi said in his book Madkhal al-Sunan: "Chapter on mentioning the statements of the Companions when they differ."

Al-Shafi'i said: "The statements of the Companions when they differ, they are to be referred to what agrees with the Book and the Sunnah or consensus, if it is more sound in analogy. And when one of them makes a statement that is not known to have any agreement or disagreement from another of them, I follow his statement if I do not find a Book, a Sunnah, a consensus, or anything in its meaning that is judged by its ruling, or if there is an analogy alongside it."

Al-Bayhaqi said, and al-Shafi'i said in his book on his disagreement with Malik: "When the Book and the Sunnah are present, the excuse of one who has heard them is certain unless he follows them. If that is not the case, we turn to the statements of the Companions or of one of them. Then, if we turn to imitation (taqlid), the statements of the Imams Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman are more beloved to us. This applies when we do not find in the disagreement any indication pointing to what is closest to the Book and the Sunnah among the disagreements. Then we follow the statement that has the indication. For the statement of an Imam is well known to bind the people. Whoever's statement binds the people is more widely known than one who gives a verdict to a man or a group. The Imam may adopt his verdict or abandon it. Most verdict-givers issue verdicts to the select few in their houses and gatherings, and the common people do not care about what they said as much as they care about what the Imam said. We have found that the Imams are appointed and asked about knowledge from the Book and the Sunnah regarding what they intended to say, and they say, then they are informed of something contrary to their statement. They accept from the informant, and they do not disdain to return to the truth, out of their piety before Allah and their virtue. If it is not found from the Imams, then the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in religion are in a position of trust, and we adopt their statements. Following them is more worthy for us than following those after them."

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Knowledge has levels. The first is the Book and the Sunnah. The second is consensus concerning what is not a Book or a Sunnah. The third is that a Companion says something, and no opponent is known among the Companions. The fourth is the disagreement of the Companions. The fifth is analogy (qiyas)." All of this is his statement in the Jadid.

قالَ البَيْهَقِيُّ بَعْدَ أنْ ذَكَرَ هَذا: وفي الرِّسالَةِ القَدِيمَةِ لِلشّافِعِيِّ (al-Shafi'i) - بَعْدَ ذِكْرِ الصَّحابَةِ وتَعْظِيمِهِمْ - قالَ: وهو فَوْقَنا في كُلِّ عِلْمٍ واجْتِهادٍ ووَرَعٍ وعَقْلٍ، وأمْرٍ اسْتُدْرِكَ بِهِ عِلْمٌ، وآراؤُهم لَنا أحْمَدُ، وأوْلى بِنا مِن رَأْيِنا، ومَن أدْرَكْنا مِمَّنْ تُرْضى أوْ حُكِيَ لَنا عَنْهُ بِبَلَدِنا صارُوا فِيما لَمْ يَعْلَمُوا فِيهِ سُنَّةً إلى قَوْلِهِمْ إنْ اجْتَمَعُوا أوْ قَوْلِ بَعْضِهِمْ إنْ تَفَرَّقُوا، وكَذا نَقُولُ، ولَمْ نَخْرُجْ مِن أقْوالِهِمْ كُلِّهِمْ.

قالَ: وإذا قالَ الرَّجُلانِ مِنهم في شَيْءٍ قَوْلَيْنِ نَظَرْت، فَإنْ كانَ قَوْلُ أحَدِهِما أشْبَهَ بِالكِتابِ والسُّنَّةِ أخَذْت بِهِ، لِأنَّ مَعَهُ شَيْئًا قَوِيًّا؛ فَإنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ عَلى واحِدٍ مِن القَوْلَيْنِ دَلالَةً بِما وصَفْت كانَ قَوْلُ الأئِمَّةِ أبِي بَكْرٍ وعُمَرَ وعُثْمانَ أرْجَحَ عِنْدَنا مِن واحِدٍ لَوْ خالَفَهم غَيْرُ إمامٍ.

قالَ البَيْهَقِيُّ: وقالَ في مَوْضِعٍ آخَرَ: فَإنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ عَلى القَوْلِ دَلالَةٌ مِن كِتابٍ ولا سُنَّةٍ كانَ قَوْلُ أبِي بَكْرٍ وعُمَرَ وعُثْمانَ أحَبَّ إلَيَّ مِن قَوْلِ غَيْرِهِمْ، فَإنْ اخْتَلَفُوا صِرْنا إلى القَوْلِ الَّذِي عَلَيْهِ دَلالَةٌ، وقَلَّما يَخْلُو اخْتِلافُهم مِن ذَلِكَ، وإنْ اخْتَلَفُوا بِلا دَلالَةٍ نَظَرْنا إلى الأكْثَرِ، فَإنْ تَكافَئُوا نَظَرْنا أحْسَنَ أقاوِيلِهِمْ مَخْرَجًا عِنْدَنا، وإنْ وجَدْنا لِلْمُفْتِينَ في زَمانِنا أوْ قَبْلَهُ إجْماعًا في شَيْءٍ تَبِعْناهُ (ijma', consensus)، فَإذا نَزَلَتْ نازِلَةٌ لَمْ نَجِدْ فِيها واحِدَةً مِن هَذِهِ الأُمُورِ فَلَيْسَ إلّا إجْهادُ الرَّأْيِ (ijtihad, independent reasoning)، فَهَذا كَلامُ الشّافِعِيِّ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ - ورَضِيَ عَنْهُ بِنَصِّهِ، ونَحْنُ نَشْهَدُ بِاللَّهِ أنَّهُ لَمْ يَرْجِعْ عَنْهُ، بَلْ كَلامُهُ في الجَدِيدِ (al-Jadid, the New Doctrine) مُطابِقٌ لِهَذا مُوافِقٌ لَهُ كَما تَقَدَّمَ ذِكْرُ لَفْظِهِ، وقَدْ قالَ في الجَدِيدِ في قَتْلِ الرّاهِبِ: إنّهُ القِياسُ عِنْدَهُ، ولَكِنْ أتْرُكُهُ لِقَوْلِ أبِي بَكْرٍ الصِّدِّيقِ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ -. فَقَدْ أخْبَرَنا أنَّهُ تَرَكَ القِياسَ (qiyas, analogy) الَّذِي هو دَلِيلٌ عِنْدَهُ لِقَوْلِ الصّاحِبِ، فَكَيْفَ يَتْرُكُ مُوجِبَ الدَّلِيلِ لِغَيْرِ دَلِيلٍ؟ وقالَ: في الضِّلَعِ بَعِيرٌ، قُلْتُهُ تَقْلِيدًا لِعُمَرَ، وقالَ في مَوْضِعٍ آخَرَ: قُلْتُهُ تَقْلِيدًا لِعُثْمانَ، وقالَ في الفَرائِضِ: هَذا مَذْهَبٌ تَلَقَّيْناهُ عَنْ زَيْدٍ. ولا تَسْتَوْحِشْ مِن لَفْظَةِ التَّقْلِيدِ (taqlid, imitation) في كَلامِهِ، وتَظُنَّ أنَّها تَنْفِي كَوْنَ قَوْلِهِ حُجَّةً بِناءً عَلى ما تَلَقَّيْتُهُ مِن اصْطِلاحِ المُتَأخِّرِينَ أنَّ التَّقْلِيدَ قَبُولُ قَوْلِ الغَيْرِ بِغَيْرِ حُجَّةٍ، فَهَذا اصْطِلاحٌ حادِثٌ، وقَدْ صَرَّحَ الشّافِعِيُّ في مَوْضِعِ مِن كَلامِهِ بِتَقْلِيدِ خَبَرِ الواحِدِ فَقالَ: قُلْت هَذا تَقْلِيدًا لِلْخَبَرِ، وأئِمَّةُ الإسْلامِ كُلُّهم عَلى قَبُولِ قَوْلِ الصَّحابِيِّ.

قالَ نُعَيْمُ بْنُ حَمّادٍ: ثنا ابْنُ المُبارَكِ قالَ: سَمِعْت أبا حَنِيفَةَ يَقُولُ: إذا جاءَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ ﷺ فَعَلى الرَّأْسِ والعَيْنِ، وإذا جاءَ عَنْ الصَّحابَةِ نَخْتارُ مِن قَوْلِهِمْ، وإذا جاءَ عَنْ التّابِعِينَ زاحَمْناهم.

وَذَهَبَ بَعْضُ المُتَأخِّرِينَ مِن الحَنَفِيَّةِ والشّافِعِيَّةِ والمالِكِيَّةِ والحَنابِلَةِ، وأكْثَرُ المُتَكَلِّمِينَ إلى أنَّهُ لَيْسَ بِحُجَّةٍ، وذَهَبَ بَعْضُ الفُقَهاءِ إلى أنَّهُ إنْ خالَفَ القِياسَ فَهو حُجَّةٌ، وإلّا فَلا، قالُوا: لِأنَّهُ إذا خالَفَ القِياسَ لَمْ يَكُنْ إلّا عَنْ تَوْقِيفٍ (tawqif, divine stipulation) وعَلى هَذا فَهو حُجَّةٌ، وإنْ خالَفَهُ صَحابِيٌّ آخَرُ، واَلَّذِينَ قالُوا "لَيْسَ بِحُجَّةٍ" قالُوا: لِأنَّ الصَّحابِيَّ مُجْتَهِدٌ مِن المُجْتَهِدِينَ يَجُوزُ عَلَيْهِ الخَطَأُ فَلا يَجِبُ تَقْلِيدُهُ، ولا يَكُونُ قَوْلُهُ حُجَّةً كَسائِرِ المُجْتَهِدِينَ، ولِأنَّ الأدِلَّةَ الدّالَّةَ عَلى بُطْلانِ التَّقْلِيدِ تَعُمُّ تَقْلِيدَ الصَّحابَةِ ومَن دُونَهُمْ، ولِأنَّ التّابِعِيَّ إذا أدْرَكَ عَصْرَ الصَّحابَةِ اعْتَدَّ بِخِلافِهِ عِنْدَ أكْثَرِ النّاسِ، فَكَيْفَ يَكُونُ قَوْلُ الواحِدِ حُجَّةً عَلَيْهِ؟ ولِأنَّ الأدِلَّةَ قَدْ انْحَصَرَتْ في الكِتابِ والسُّنَّةِ والإجْماعِ والقِياسِ والِاسْتِصْحابِ (istishab, presumption of continuity)، وقَوْلُ الصَّحابِيِّ لَيْسَ واحِدًا مِنها، ولِأنَّ امْتِيازَهُ بِكَوْنِهِ أفْضَلَ، وأعْلَمَ وأتْقى لا يُوجِبُ وُجُوبَ اتِّباعِهِ عَلى مُجْتَهِدٍ آخَرَ مِن عُلَماءِ التّابِعِينَ بِالنِّسْبَةِ إلى مَن بَعْدَهم.

[فصل: الأدِلَّةُ عَلى وُجُوبِ اتِّباعِ الصَّحابَةِ]

فَأمّا الأوَّلُ فَمِن وُجُوهٍ: أحَدُها: ما احْتَجَّ بِهِ مالِكٌ، وهو قَوْله تَعالى: ﴿والسّابِقُونَ الأوَّلُونَ مِنَ المُهاجِرِينَ والأنْصارِ والَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوهم بِإحْسانٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهم ورَضُوا عَنْهُ وأعَدَّ لَهم جَنّاتٍ تَجْرِي تَحْتَها الأنْهارُ خالِدِينَ فِيها أبَدًا ذَلِكَ الفَوْزُ العَظِيمُ﴾ [التوبة: ١٠٠] (The foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in excellence: Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him, and He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great achievement.)

فَوَجْهُ الدَّلالَةِ أنَّ اللَّهَ تَعالى أثْنى عَلى مَن اتَّبَعَهُمْ، فَإذا قالُوا قَوْلًا فاتَّبَعَهم مُتَّبِعٌ عَلَيْهِ قَبْلَ أنْ يَعْرِفَ صِحَّتَهُ فَهو مُتَّبِعٌ لَهُمْ، فَيَجِبُ أنْ يَكُونَ مَحْمُودًا عَلى ذَلِكَ، وأنْ يَسْتَحِقَّ الرِّضْوانَ، ولَوْ كانَ اتِّباعُهم تَقْلِيدًا مَحْضًا كَتَقْلِيدِ بَعْضِ المُفْتِينَ لَمْ يَسْتَحِقَّ مَن اتَّبَعَهم الرِّضْوانَ إلّا أنْ يَكُونَ عامِّيًّا، فَأمّا العُلَماءُ المُجْتَهِدُونَ فَلا يَجُوزُ لَهم اتِّباعُهم حِينَئِذٍ.

فَإنْ قِيلَ: اتِّباعُهم هو أنْ يَقُولَ ما قالُوا بِالدَّلِيلِ، وهو سُلُوكُ سَبِيلِ الِاجْتِهادِ؛ لِأنَّهم إنّما قالُوا بِالِاجْتِهادِ، والدَّلِيلُ عَلَيْهِ قَوْلُهُ ﴿بِإحْسانٍ﴾ ومَن قَلَّدَهم لَمْ يَتَّبِعْهم بِإحْسانٍ لِأنَّهُ لَوْ كانَ مُطْلَقُ الِاتِّباعِ مَحْمُودًا لَمْ يُفَرِّقْ بَيْنَ الِاتِّباعِ بِإحْسانٍ أوْ بِغَيْرِ إحْسانٍ، وأيْضًا فَيَجُوزُ أنْ يُرادُ بِهِ اتِّباعُهم في أُصُولِ الدِّينِ، وقَوْلُهُ ﴿بِإحْسانٍ﴾ أيْ بِالتِزامِ الفَرائِضِ واجْتِنابِ المَحارِمِ، ويَكُونُ المَقْصُودُ أنَّ السّابِقِينَ قَدْ وجَبَ لَهم الرِّضْوانُ، وإنْ أساءُوا؛ لِقَوْلِهِ ﷺ «وَما يُدْرِيك أنَّ اللَّهَ قَدْ اطَّلَعَ عَلى أهْلِ بَدْرٍ فَقالَ: اعْمَلُوا ما شِئْتُمْ فَقَدْ غَفَرْت لَكُمْ» (ﷺ) [ "And what would make you know that Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do as you wish, for I have forgiven you." ]، وأيْضًا فالثَّناءُ عَلى مَن اتَّبَعَهم كُلَّهُمْ، وذَلِكَ اتِّباعُهم فِيما أجْمَعُوا عَلَيْهِ، وأيْضًا فالثَّناءُ عَلى مَن اتَّبَعَهم لا يَقْتَضِي وُجُوبَهُ، وإنَّما يَدُلُّ عَلى جَوازِ تَقْلِيدِهِمْ، وذَلِكَ دَلِيلُ جَوازِ تَقْلِيدِ العالِمِ كَما هو مَذْهَبُ طائِفَةٍ مِن العُلَماءِ، أوْ تَقْلِيدِ الأعْلَمِ كَقَوْلِ طائِفَةٍ أُخْرى.

أمّا الدَّلِيلُ عَلى وُجُوبِ اتِّباعِهِمْ فَلَيْسَ في الآيَةِ ما يَقْتَضِيهِ.

فالجَوابُ مِن وُجُوهِ: أحَدُها: أنَّ الِاتِّباعَ لا يَسْتَلْزِمُ الِاجْتِهادَ لِوُجُوهٍ:
أحَدُها: أنَّ الِاتِّباعَ المَأْمُورَ بِهِ في القُرْآنِ كَقَوْلِهِ ﴿فاتَّبِعُونِي يُحْبِبْكُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ [آل عمران: ٣١] (Follow me, and Allah will love you) ﴿واتَّبِعُوهُ لَعَلَّكم تَهْتَدُونَ﴾ [الأعراف: ١٥٨] (And follow him that you may be guided) ﴿وَيَتَّبِعْ غَيْرَ سَبِيلِ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ [النساء: ١١٥] (And follows other than the way of the believers) ونَحْوُهُ لا يَتَوَقَّفُ عَلى الِاسْتِدْلالِ عَلى صِحَّةِ القَوْلِ مَعَ الِاسْتِغْناءِ عَنْ القائِلِ.
الثّانِي: أنَّهُ لَوْ كانَ المُرادُ اتِّباعَهم في الِاسْتِدْلالِ والِاجْتِهادِ لَمْ يَكُنْ فَرْقٌ بَيْنَ السّابِقِينَ وبَيْنَ جَمِيعِ الخَلائِقِ؛ لِأنَّ اتِّباعَ مُوجِبِ الدَّلِيلِ يَجِبُ أنْ يَتَّبِعَ فِيهِ كُلُّ أحَدٍ، فَمَن قالَ قَوْلًا بِدَلِيلٍ صَحِيحٍ وجَبَ مُوافَقَتُهُ فِيهِ.
الثّالِثُ: أنَّهُ إمّا أنْ تَجُوزَ مُخالَفَتُهم في قَوْلِهِمْ بَعْدَ الِاسْتِدْلالِ أوْ لا تَجُوزُ، فَإنْ لَمْ تَجُزْ فَهو المَطْلُوبُ، وإنْ جازَتْ مُخالَفَتُهم فَقَدْ خُولِفُوا في خُصُوصِ الحُكْمِ واتَّبَعُوا في أحْسَنِ الِاسْتِدْلالِ، فَلَيْسَ جَعْلُ مَن فَعَلَ ذَلِكَ مُتْبِعًا لِمُوافَقَتِهِمْ في الِاسْتِدْلالِ بِأوْلى مِن جَعْلِهِ مُخالِفًا لِمُخالَفَتِهِ في عَيْنِ الحُكْمِ.
الرّابِعُ: أنَّ مَن خالَفَهم في الحُكْمِ الَّذِي أفْتَوْا بِهِ لا يَكُونُ مُتَّبِعًا لَهم أصْلًا، بِدَلِيلِ أنَّ مَن خالَفَ مُجْتَهِدًا مِن المُجْتَهِدِينَ في مَسْألَةٍ بَعْدَ اجْتِهادٍ لا يَصِحُّ أنْ يُقالَ "اتَّبِعْهُ"، وإنْ أطْلَقَ ذَلِكَ فَلا بُدَّ مِن تَقْيِيدِهِ بِأنْ يُقالَ اتَّبِعْهُ في الِاسْتِدْلالِ أوْ الِاجْتِهادِ.
الخامِسُ: أنَّ الِاتِّباعَ افْتِعالٌ مِن اتَّبَعَ، وكَوْنُ الإنْسانِ تابِعًا لِغَيْرِهِ نَوْعَ افْتِقارٍ إلَيْهِ ومَشْيٍ خَلْفَهُ، وكُلُّ واحِدٍ مِن المُجْتَهِدِينَ المُسْتَدِلِّينَ لَيْسَ تَبَعًا لِلْآخَرِ ولا مُفْتَقِرًا إلَيْهِ بِمُجَرَّدِ ذَلِكَ حَتّى يَسْتَشْعِرَ مُوافَقَتَهُ والِانْقِيادَ لَهُ، ولِهَذا لا يَصِحُّ أنْ يُقالَ لِمَن وافَقَ رَجُلًا في اجْتِهادِهِ أوْ فَتْواهُ اتِّفاقًا إنّهُ مُتَّبِعٌ لَهُ.
السّادِسُ: أنَّ الآيَةَ قُصِدَ بِها مَدْحُ السّابِقِينَ والثَّناءُ عَلَيْهِمْ، وبَيانُ اسْتِحْقاقِهِمْ أنْ يَكُونُوا أئِمَّةً مَتْبُوعِينَ، وبِتَقْدِيرِ ألّا يَكُونَ قَوْلُهم مُوجِبًا لِلْمُوافَقَةِ ولا مانِعًا مِن المُخالَفَةِ - بَلْ إنّما يَتَّبِعُ القِياسَ مَثَلًا - لا يَكُونُ لَهم هَذا المَنصِبُ، ولا يَسْتَحِقُّونَ هَذا المَدْحَ والثَّناءَ.
السّابِعُ: أنَّ مَن خالَفَهم في خُصُوصِ الحُكْمِ فَلَمْ يَتَّبِعْهم في ذَلِكَ الحُكْمِ ولا فِيما اسْتَدَلُّوا بِهِ عَلى ذَلِكَ الحُكْمِ فَلا يَكُونُ مُتَّبِعًا لَهم بِمُجَرَّدِ مُشارَكَتِهِمْ في صِفَةٍ عامَّةٍ، وهي مُطْلَقُ الِاسْتِدْلالِ والِاجْتِهادِ، ولا سِيَّما وتِلْكَ الصِّفَةُ العامَّةُ لا اخْتِصاصَ لَها بِهِ؛ لِأنَّ ما يَنْفِي الِاتِّباعَ أخَصُّ مِمّا يُثْبِتُهُ.

وَإذا وُجِدَ الفارِقُ الأخَصُّ والجامِعُ الأعَمُّ - وكِلاهُما مُؤَثِّرٌ - كانَ التَّفْرِيقُ رِعايَةً لِلْفارِقِ أوْلى مِن الجَمْعِ رِعايَةً لِلْجامِعِ، وأمّا قَوْلُهُ: ﴿بِإحْسانٍ﴾ فَلَيْسَ المُرادُ بِهِ أنْ يَجْتَهِدَ، وافَقَ أوْ خالَفَ؛ لِأنَّهُ إذا خالَفَ لَمْ يَتَّبِعْهم فَضْلًا عَنْ أنْ يَكُونَ بِإحْسانٍ، ولِأنَّ مُطْلَقَ الِاجْتِهادِ لَيْسَ فِيهِ اتِّباعٌ لَهُمْ، لَكِنَّ الِاتِّباعَ لَهم اسْمٌ يَدْخُلُ فِيهِ كُلُّ مَن وافَقَهم في الِاعْتِقادِ والقَوْلِ، فَلا بُدَّ مَعَ ذَلِكَ أنْ يَكُونَ المُتَّبِعُ مُحْسِنًا بِأداءِ الفَرائِضِ واجْتِنابِ المَحارِمِ؛ لِئَلّا يَقَعَ الِاغْتِرارُ بِمُجَرَّدِ المُوافَقَةِ قَوْلًا، وأيْضًا فَلا بُدَّ أنْ يُحْسِنَ المُتَّبِعُ لَهم القَوْلَ فِيهِمْ، ولا يَقْدَحُ فِيهِمْ، اشْتَرَطَ اللَّهُ ذَلِكَ لِعِلْمِهِ بِأنْ سَيَكُونُ أقْوامٌ يَنالُونَ مِنهم.

وَهَذا مِثْلُ قَوْله تَعالى بَعْدَ أنْ ذَكَرَ المُهاجِرِينَ والأنْصارَ: ﴿والَّذِينَ جاءُوا مِن بَعْدِهِمْ يَقُولُونَ رَبَّنا اغْفِرْ لَنا ولإخْوانِنا الَّذِينَ سَبَقُونا بِالإيمانِ ولا تَجْعَلْ في قُلُوبِنا غِلا لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ [الحشر: ١٠] (And those who came after them say: Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and put not in our hearts any resentment toward those who have believed.) وأمّا تَخْصِيصُ اتِّباعِهِمْ بِأُصُولِ الدِّينِ دُونَ فُرُوعِهِ فَلا يَصِحُّ؛ لِأنَّ الِاتِّباعَ عامٌّ، ولِأنَّ مَن اتَّبَعَهم في أُصُولِ الدِّينِ فَقَطْ لَوْ كانَ مُتَّبِعًا لَهم عَلى الإطْلاقِ لَكُنّا مُتَّبِعِينَ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ مِن أهْلِ الكِتابِ، ولَمْ يَكُنْ فَرْقٌ بَيْنَ اتِّباعِ السّابِقِينَ مِن هَذِهِ الأُمَّةِ وغَيْرِها.

وَأيْضًا فَإنَّهُ إذا قِيلَ "فُلانٌ يَتَّبِعُ فُلانًا، واتَّبِعْ فُلانًا، وأنا مُتَّبِعٌ فُلانًا"، ولَمْ يُقَيِّدْ ذَلِكَ بِقَرِينَةٍ لَفْظِيَّةٍ ولا حالِيَّةٍ فَإنَّهُ يَقْتَضِي اتِّباعَهُ في كُلِّ الأُمُورِ الَّتِي يَتَأتّى فِيها الِاتِّباعُ؛ لِأنَّ مَن اتَّبَعَهُ في حالٍ وخالَفَهُ في أُخْرى لَمْ يَكُنْ وصْفُهُ بِأنَّهُ مُتَّبِعٌ أوْلى مِن وصْفِهِ بِأنَّهُ مُخالِفٌ؛ ولِأنَّ الرِّضْوانَ حُكْمٌ تَعَلَّقَ بِاتِّباعِهِمْ، فَيَكُونُ الِاتِّباعُ سَبَبًا لَهُ؛ لِأنَّ الحُكْمَ المُعَلَّقَ بِما هو مُشْتَقٌّ يَقْتَضِي أنَّ ما مِنهُ الِاشْتِقاقُ سَبَبٌ، وإذا كانَ اتِّباعُهم سَبَبًا لِلرِّضْوانِ اقْتَضى الحُكْمَ في جَمِيعِ مَوارِدِهِ، ولا اخْتِصاصَ لِلِاتِّباعِ بِحالٍ دُونَ حالٍ، ولِأنَّ الِاتِّباعَ يُؤْذِنُ بِكَوْنِ الإنْسانِ تَبَعًا لِغَيْرِهِ وفَرْعًا عَلَيْهِ، وأُصُولُ الدِّينِ لَيْسَتْ كَذَلِكَ ولِأنَّ الآيَةَ تَضَمَّنَتْ الثَّناءَ عَلَيْهِمْ وجَعْلَهم أئِمَّةً لِمَن بَعْدَهُمْ، فَلَوْ لَمْ يَتَناوَلْ إلّا اتِّباعَهم في أُصُولِ الدِّينِ دُونَ الشَّرائِعِ لَمْ يَكُونُوا أئِمَّةً في ذَلِكَ لِأنَّ ذَلِكَ مَعْلُومٌ مَعَ قَطْعِ النَّظَرِ عَنْ اتِّباعِهِمْ.

(فَصْلٌ)

وَأمّا قَوْلُهم "إنّ الثَّناءَ عَلى مَن اتَّبَعَهم كُلَّهم" فَنَقُولُ: الآيَةُ اقْتَضَتْ الثَّناءَ عَلى مَن يَتَّبِعُ كُلَّ واحِدٍ مِنهُمْ، كَما أنَّ قَوْلَهُ ﴿والسّابِقُونَ الأوَّلُونَ مِنَ المُهاجِرِينَ والأنْصارِ والَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوهُمْ﴾ يَقْتَضِي حُصُولَ الرِّضْوانِ لِكُلِّ واحِدٍ مِن السّابِقِينَ واَلَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوهم في قَوْلِهِ ﴿رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهم ورَضُوا عَنْهُ وأعَدَّ لَهم جَنّاتٍ تَجْرِي﴾ وكَذَلِكَ في قَوْلِهِ ﴿اتَّبَعُوهُمْ﴾ لِأنَّهُ حُكْمٌ عَلَّقَ عَلَيْهِمْ في هَذِهِ الآيَةِ، فَقَدْ تَناوَلَهم مُجْتَمِعِينَ ومُنْفَرِدِينَ.

Also, the principle regarding rulings attached to general names is that each individual member of those named groups is included. An example is His saying, ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ [al-An'am: 72], and His saying, ﴿Certainly Allah was pleased with the believers﴾ [al-Fath: 18], and the Exalted's saying, ﴿Be mindful of Allah and be with the truthful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 119]. Also, rulings attached to a collective are expressed with a name that refers to the collective as a whole and not to its individuals, such as His saying, ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], His saying, ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110], and His saying, ﴿and follows other than the way of the believers﴾ [al-Nisa': 115]. The word "ummah" (nation) and the phrase "the way of the believers" cannot be distributed over the individual members of the nation or of the believers, unlike the word "al-sabiqun" (the foremost), which applies to each individual of the foremost.

Also, the verse encompasses following them when they are gathered and when they are separate, in every possible case. Whoever follows their community when they are gathered, and follows their individuals in what he finds from them that none of the others among them opposes, has indeed truly followed the foremost. But whoever opposes some of the foremost cannot correctly be said to have "followed the foremost," because of his opposition to some of them, especially if he opposes this one once and that one at another time. Through this the answer becomes clear regarding their following when they disagree. Their following in such cases means adopting one of those opinions through ijtihad (independent reasoning) and inference, since they all agree that each of those opinions is permissible for whoever his ijtihad leads to. Thus he has also intended to follow them. But if a man states an opinion that none of the others opposes, one does not know that the foremost permitted the contrary of that opinion. Also, the verse requires following them absolutely.

Suppose the seeker encounters a text that contradicts the view of one of them. We know that if he had found that text, he would not have turned away from it. But if we hold an opinion, it may be permissible for it to be contradicted.

Also, if their following were only in matters on which they all agreed, then following them would only be achieved in what is known to be part of the religion of Islam by necessity, because the foremost early Muslims were a great multitude, and it is not known that they all agreed except on that. This case would then be the same as the previous one, and its invalidity has already been established, since following in that matter has no effect. Also, some of the foremost died during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and at that time there was no need to follow them, since one was independent of them by the words of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Furthermore, even if we supposed someone who followed them at that time, he would be among the foremost. The upshot is that the later generations cannot follow all of the foremost. Also, knowing the view of all the foremost is nearly impossible, so how could they all be followed in something that is hardly known?

Also, they only deserved the station of leadership and of being emulated by virtue of being the foremost, and this quality exists in each one of them. Therefore each of them must be a leader for the God-fearing, just as each of them has earned Allah's good pleasure and Paradise.

(Section)

As for his statement, "There is nothing in it that makes following them obligatory," we say: the verse indicates Allah's good pleasure toward whoever follows them in excellence. It has been established that speaking about religion without knowledge is forbidden. Therefore following them is not speaking without knowledge; rather it is speaking with knowledge, and this is the aim. In that case, it makes no difference whether it is called taqlid (blind imitation) or ijtihad. Also, if one scholar's taqlid of another scholar is forbidden, as the Shafi'is and the Hanbalis hold, then following them is not taqlid, because it is praiseworthy. But if their taqlid is permissible, or their taqlid is an exception to the forbidden taqlid, no one has said that the taqlid of scholars is among the causes of Allah's good pleasure. It is thus known that their taqlid lies outside this. This is because the taqlid of a scholar, even if permissible, may be abandoned in favor of another's view or in favor of ijtihad, which is also permissible by consensus, and a permissible act does not merit Allah's good pleasure. Also, Allah's good pleasure is the ultimate goal, which is attained only through the most excellent deeds, and it is known that the taqlid whose opposite is permissible is not the most excellent deed; rather ijtihad is better than it. Thus it is known that following them is the most excellent course in a matter on which they and those after them differed, and that following them rather than those after them is what brings about Allah's good pleasure. There is no doubt that the preponderance of one of two opinions makes following it obligatory. [And their opinion is more preponderant], beyond doubt, and in matters of ijtihad a person does not have free choice between the two views.

Also, Allah praised those who followed them in excellence. Taqlid is the duty of the common people. As for scholars, it is either permissible for them or forbidden, since ijtihad is better for them without any disagreement, and it is obligatory upon them. If following them were meant as the taqlid whose opposite is permissible, the common people would have the greatest share in that, and the share of the scholars of the nation from this verse would be the meanest share. It is known that this is corrupt. Also, Allah's good pleasure toward those who followed them is evidence that their following is correct and not erroneous. For if it were erroneous, the best outcome for its adherent would be to be pardoned for it, since the one who errs is closer to being pardoned than to being pleased with. If it is correct, following it is obligatory, because the opposite of the correct is erroneous, and error is forbidden to follow once it is known to be erroneous, and it is known that it is erroneous when the correct view is its opposite. Also, if following them brings about Allah's good pleasure, then abandoning following them does not bring about His good pleasure, because the reward does not require the existence of a thing and its opposite, nor its existence and its non-existence, since it would remain without effect on that reward. If in a matter there are two views, one of which brings about good pleasure and the other does not, then the truth is what brings it about, and this is what was sought. Also, seeking Allah's good pleasure is obligatory, because if His good pleasure is not attained, then either His wrath or His pardon follows, and pardon only occurs when the cause of a sin exists, and engaging in that is not permitted except by a text. If His good pleasure lies only in following them, and following His good pleasure is obligatory, then following them is obligatory. Also, He only praised the one who follows them with good pleasure and did not explicitly state obligation, because making following obligatory applies to following in actions, and it requires forbidding opposition to them absolutely, which would then entail blaming the one who errs, and that is not the case. As for opinions, there is no basis for opposing them once it is established that there is Allah's good pleasure in them. Also, when it is established that an opinion contains Allah's good pleasure, Allah's good pleasure does not lie in its opposite. This differs from actions, for Allah's good pleasure may lie in differing actions, and in doing or abandoning an act depending on two intentions and two circumstances. Beliefs and opinions are not like that. So when it is established that in their opinion there is Allah's good pleasure, the truth and correctness can only be that, and therefore following it is obligatory.

If it is said: the foremost are those who prayed toward both qiblas, or they are the people of the Pledge of al-Ridwan and those before them. What is the evidence for following those who embraced Islam after that? It is said: once the obligation to follow the people of the Pledge of al-Ridwan is established, that is the greatest objective. Moreover, no one holds a distinction between them. Every Companion is among the foremost in relation to those after them.

(Precious Benefit)

The expression "ʿaraftu kadha" (I knew such-and-such) originally serves to distinguish a thing and specify it, so that it appears to the mind singled out from other things. This root implies height and manifestness, as in ʿurf al-shayʾ (the top of a thing), from which comes al-aʿraf (the heights), and ʿurf al-dik (the comb of the rooster).

As for ʿalima ("to know"), it is applied to compound things, not to the distinguishing of single meanings. Its sense of composition is the attribution of a quality to a locus. You know Zayd in his individual self, and you know the meaning of standing in its individual self, then you attribute standing to Zayd; the attribution of standing to Zayd is the composition, and it is the object of knowledge.

If you say: "ʿalimtu" (I knew), its object comprises three meanings: a locus, a quality, and the attribution of the quality to the locus, and these are three known things. The attribution of knowledge (ʿilm) to God, rather than knowledge of acquaintance (maʿrifa), is what is at issue. Having understood this, some of the theologians (mutakallimun) said: Only ʿilm, not maʿrifa, may be attributed to God Most High, because His knowledge relates to all things, compound and simple, with a single relation, unlike the knowledge of created beings, whose acquaintance with a simple thing and whose knowledge of it are different from their knowledge and acquaintance with another thing. This is a construction on their part on the basis that God Most High knows all known things with a single knowledge, and that His knowledge of the truthfulness of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is identical with His knowledge of the falsehood of Musaylima the Liar. However, the position of the verifying scholars (muhaqqiqu al-nuzzar) is contrary to this view: knowledge is multiple and differs according to the multiplicity and difference of the known things, so every known thing has its own knowledge. To refute the opinion of those people and to mention the strong proofs for the correctness of these people's view has a more appropriate place. On this basis, the difference between attributing ʿilm to Him, Exalted, and not attributing maʿrifa does not return to the singularity or compositeness of the object of knowledge, but returns to maʿrifa itself and its meaning. For in its established usage, maʿrifa is used only of what was previously conceived, after forgetting, inattention, or the heart's turning away. When it is conceived and present in the mind, one says ʿarafahu (he recognized him), or his description is given to him, and he has not seen him; when he sees him with that description and it becomes specified in him, one says ʿarafahu. Do you not see that if a man's face is absent from you and then you see him after a time and realize that it is him, you say ʿarraftuhu (I recognized him)? Likewise one says ʿarafat al-lafza (I recognized the word), ʿarafat al-diyar (I recognized the abodes), ʿarafat al-manzil (I recognized the dwelling), ʿarafat al-tariq (I recognized the road). The secret of the matter is that maʿrifa is for distinguishing what the known is mixed with another and thus confused; maʿrifa is then a distinguishing and specifying of it. From this is His saying: ﴿They recognize him as they recognize their sons﴾.

For they had, before seeing him, a description of him that corresponded to his person when seen, and the comparison "as they recognize their sons" came by way of parallel phrasing and likening one certainty to the other. Consider it.

We have expounded this in the book (al-Tuhfa al-Makkiyya), and mentioned in it secrets and benefits that no author could comprehensively contain.

As for what they claim, that ʿalima may mean ʿarafa, and their citing such verses as His saying: ﴿You do not know them; We know them﴾ and His saying: ﴿And others besides them, whom you do not know; God knows them﴾, what prompted them to this is that they saw ʿalima transitive to a single object, and this is the essence of ʿirfan (recognition). So this is a clear proof. It has been said by some people that the transitivity of the verb of knowing in these verses and their like to a single object does not take it out of being knowledge in the true sense; rather, it is not transitive to a single object in the manner of ʿarafa, but by way of elision and abbreviation. So His saying: ﴿You do not know them; We know them﴾ does not negate knowing their persons and names, but negates knowing their enmity and hypocrisy, as the preceding discourse shows. Likewise His saying: ﴿And others besides them, whom you do not know; God knows them﴾. For they may have recognized them yet not known them as enemies to them, so the knowledge relates to the quality attributed to the described, not to his specific self and essence. He said this. But whoever says that ʿalima means ʿarafa because it is transitive to one object in wording is like one who says that saʾala (to ask) is transitive to non-rational things by saying: "I asked the wall" and "I asked the house," and cites His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾. He said: This is merely ignorance of metaphor and elision, and so is what preceded. But what these people said is not strong, for God, Glorified is He, negated from His Messenger knowledge of the persons of those hypocrites; this is the plain sense of the wording. The negation of knowledge of their hypocrisy came only by way of implication, for he (ﷺ) knew that hypocrisy existed in specific persons and was present among others, yet did not know their individuals. The intent is not that their persons were known and recognized by him while they had concealed hypocrisy and he did not know it of them. The wording does not indicate that in any way. The apparent and indeed the required meaning is that if he had known their persons, he would have recognized them by their marks and in the import of speech, and the hypocrisy of one who displays Islam to him while concealing enmity toward him and enmity toward God, Mighty and Majestic, would not have been hidden from him. What makes this clearer is the other verse, for His saying: ﴿You terrify thereby the enemy of God and your enemy, and others besides them whom you do not know﴾, concerning whom there are two opinions:

The first: they are the jinn who support their fellows among mankind in fighting God and His Messenger. On this view the verse is explicit that knowledge there means acquaintance, and it cannot be said that they recognized the persons of those but were ignorant of their enmity, as could be said in the case of humans.

The second: they are the hypocrites. On this view, His saying ﴿you do not know them﴾ should be understood as not knowing their persons, not as not knowing their hypocrisy, for they knew the hypocrisy of many of the hypocrites, knowing it and having no doubt of it. So it is not permissible to negate from them knowledge of what they know; rather, what is negated is knowledge of the persons of this kind. This is like His saying: ﴿You do not know them; We know them﴾. Consider it.

What makes it still clearer is that these verbs do not permit being limited to one of two objects, unlike the pattern of aʿtā (to give) and kasā (to clothe), for the reason mentioned there: these verbs relate to a relation (nisba), so both related parties must be mentioned. Unlike the pattern of aʿtā, which does not relate to a relation, so it is correct to limit it to one of its two objects. This is clear, as you see. And God knows best.

As for their comparison of "saʾaltu al-ḥaʾiṭ" and "al-dar," the gap between them is wide, for that is a question by the tongue of the state (lisan al-ḥal), which is very common in their speech. Moreover, it is not impossible that it be a question by explicit tongue of speech, as a man says to a ruined house: "I wonder what has become of your people, and I wonder what has brought you to this state?" This is not a question seeking information, but a question of wonder, grief and sorrow.

As for His saying ﴿And ask the town﴾: if "al-qarya" here is a name for the inhabitants, as it is in most of the Qur'an and speech, then there is no metaphor and no elision; and if what is meant is the dwelling, then it is by elision of the qualifier, so where is the parity and the analogy?

(Benefit)

When God wills good for a servant, He makes him one who acknowledges his own sin, who refrains from mentioning the sins of others, who is generous with what he has, who is detached from what others have, and who bears patiently the harm of others.

And if He wills evil for him, the opposite of that befalls him.

The lofty aspiration never ceases to hover around three things:

knowledge of one of the sublime attributes, the increase of which through knowing brings love, desire and contemplation; attentiveness to a favour, the increase of which through attending to it brings gratitude and obedience; and remembrance of a sin, the increase of which through remembering it brings repentance and fear. When aspiration becomes attached to anything other than these three, it wanders through the valleys of whisperings and passing thoughts.

**(Benefit)**

Both the heart and the body need to be nurtured, so that they grow, increase, reach completion and become sound. Just as the body needs to be purified and developed through wholesome foods and by avoiding what harms it, so that it grows only when it is given what benefits it and kept from what harms it, the heart does not grow, increase, or reach its proper soundness except by this same means. It has no path to this except through the Qur'an. If it reaches any of this from other sources, that is a small and meagre portion that does not secure the full aim. Likewise, a crop is not complete except through these two things, and then it is said: the crop has grown (zakā) and become complete.

Since its life and bliss cannot be complete except through its purification and cleansing, it is necessary to mention both this and that. We say:

*Zakāh* (purification, growth) in language means growth and increase in goodness, and the completeness of a thing. It is said: "The thing grew (zakā)" when it increased. God the Exalted said: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103].

Thus He combined the two matters, purification and growth, because they are inseparable. The filth of vices and sins in the heart is like the corrupt humours in the body, like the weeds in a crop, and like the dross in gold, silver, copper and iron. Just as, when the body is purged of corrupt humours, its natural faculty is freed from them and rests, performing its function without obstruction or hindrance, and so the body grows, likewise when the heart is freed from sins through repentance, it has purged itself of its confusion. The heart's will and its desire for good become unimpeded, and it rests from those corrupt pulls and bad matters. Then it grows, becomes strong and firm, sits upon the throne of its kingdom, and its rule is executed over its subjects, who hear and obey. Therefore it has no way to its growth except after its purification, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts; that is purer for them. Indeed, God is Acquainted with what they do﴾ [al-Nur: 30].

So He made growth (zakāh) to follow the lowering of the gaze and the guarding of the private parts.

**(Section: What is meant by ṣalāh)**

The root of this word in language goes back to two meanings. One is supplication and blessing (du'ā' wa tabrīk). The other is worship (ʿibādah).

From the first meaning is God's words: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow, and pray for them, for your prayer is a comfort for them﴾. And His words concerning the hypocrites: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever, nor stand at his grave﴾.

And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "If one of you is invited to a meal, let him accept; and if he is fasting, let him pray (for them)." He explained it by both meanings.[1]

It has been said: "Let him invoke blessings for them." It has also been said: "Let him perform ṣalāh there in place of eating."

It has been said that ṣalāh in language means supplication (duʿāʾ). Supplication is of two kinds: supplication of worship and supplication of request. The worshipper is one who supplicates, just as the one who asks is one who supplicates. With both meanings God's words were explained: ﴿Your Lord said: Call upon Me, and I will respond to you﴾. It was said: "Obey Me, and I will reward you." It was also said: "Ask Me, and I will give to you."

With both meanings was explained His words: ﴿When My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the call of the caller when he calls upon Me﴾.

The correct view is that supplication encompasses both kinds, and this is a univocal term (lafẓ mutawāṭi') with no homonymy (ishtirāk) in it.

From its use for supplication of worship is God's words: ﴿Say: Call upon those you claim besides God; they do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or in the earth﴾. And His words: ﴿Those whom they call upon besides God create nothing, while they themselves are created﴾. And His words: ﴿Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication﴾.

The more correct of the two views is: were it not that you call upon Him and worship Him, what would He care for you, were it not for your worship of Him? Thus the verbal noun is here an annexation to its agent. And God the Exalted said: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly. Indeed, He does not love the transgressors. And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reform, and call upon Him in fear and in hope﴾. And God the Exalted said, reporting about His prophets and messengers: ﴿Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds and would call upon Us in hope and in fear﴾.

This approach is better than the first, and the claim of disagreement over the designation of supplication is thereby removed. With this, the problems raised concerning the name of the legal ṣalāh are resolved: is it transferred from its linguistic place, making it a *ḥaqīqah sharʿiyyah* (a technical literal usage in the Law), or is it a *majāz sharʿī* (a legal figurative usage)? On this view, ṣalāh remains upon its linguistic meaning, which is supplication. Supplication is of two kinds: supplication of worship and supplication of request. The one who prays, from his takbīr to his salām, is combining supplication of worship and supplication of request. Thus he is in ṣalāh in the literal sense, not figuratively, nor by transfer. But the name ṣalāh was specialised for this particular act of worship, as with other words that the people of language and custom restrict to part of their meaning, such as "dābbah" (animal) and "ra's" (head), and the like. This is the furthest extent of the restriction of a word and its confinement to part of its original referent. For this reason it does not necessitate a transfer or an exit from its original meaning. And God knows best.

**(Section)**

This ṣalāh is from the human being.

As for God's ṣalāh upon His servants, it is of two kinds: general and specific.

The general is His ṣalāh upon His believing servants. God the Exalted said: ﴿He it is who prays upon you, and His angels﴾.

From this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) supplication with ṣalāh upon individual believers, as in his saying: "O God, send ṣalāh upon the family of Abū Awfā."

And in another hadith: "A woman said to him: Pray for me and for my husband. He said: May God send ṣalāh upon you and upon your husband."

The second kind is His specific ṣalāh: upon His prophets and messengers, and especially upon the Seal of them and the best of them, Muhammad (ﷺ). People differ regarding the meaning of God's ṣalāh, giving several opinions.

One of them: that it is mercy (raḥmah). Ismāʿīl said: Naṣr ibn ʿAlī narrated to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn Sawwār narrated to us from Juwaybir from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, who said: "The ṣalāh of God is His mercy, and the ṣalāh of the angels is supplication."

Al-Mubarrad said: The origin of ṣalāh is mercy. So from God it is mercy, and from the angels it is mercy and a request for mercy from God.

This view is the well-known one among many later scholars.

The second view: that it is His forgiveness. Ismāʿīl said: Muḥammad ibn Abī Bakr narrated to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn Sawwār narrated to us from Juwaybir from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, concerning ﴿He it is who prays upon you﴾: "The ṣalāh of God is His forgiveness, and the ṣalāh of the angels is supplication."

This view is of the same kind as the previous one. Both are weak, for several reasons.

The first: God distinguished between His ṣalāh upon His servants and His mercy. He said: ﴿And give good news to the patient, who, when calamity strikes them, say: Indeed we belong to God and indeed to Him we will return. Those are the ones upon whom are blessings (ṣalawāt) from their Lord and mercy, and those are the rightly guided﴾.

Here mercy is joined to ṣalawāt by conjunction, which requires that the two are different. This is the basic principle of conjunction.

As for their saying:

*"And he found her words false and deceitful"*

this is an anomalous and rare usage, and the most eloquent speech is not to be interpreted by it, especially since *mayn* (deceit) is more specific than *kadhib* (falsehood).

The second reason: God's ṣalāh is specific to His prophets, messengers and believing servants, whereas His mercy encompasses all things. Therefore ṣalāh is not synonymous with mercy, but mercy is one of the necessary consequences, effects and fruits of ṣalāh. Whoever explains it as mercy has explained it by one of its fruits and purposes. This occurs frequently in the interpretation of the words of the Qur'an.

The Messenger (ﷺ) explained a term by its necessary consequences and part of its meaning, as in explaining *rayb* (doubt) as *shakk* (uncertainty), since uncertainty is part of doubt. And explaining forgiveness (maghfirah) as concealment (sitr), since that is part of what forgiveness denotes. And explaining mercy as the will to do good, which is a necessary consequence of mercy. Similar examples are numerous, and we have mentioned them in the principles of tafsīr.

The third reason: there is no disagreement about the permissibility of mercy upon believers. But the early and later scholars differed on the permissibility of ṣalāh upon other than the prophets, in three opinions, which we will mention later, God willing.

Thus it is known that the two are not synonymous.

The fourth reason: if ṣalāh meant mercy, then saying "O God, have mercy upon Muḥammad and the family of Muḥammad" would fulfil the command for those who hold that ṣalāh upon the Prophet is obligatory. But the matter is not so.

The fifth reason: one does not say of someone who showed mercy to another, felt compassion for him and then fed him, gave him to drink or clothed him, that he "prayed for him (ṣallā ʿalayhi)." Rather, it is said that he has "shown mercy to him (raḥimahu)."

The sixth reason: a person may show mercy to someone he hates and is hostile to, finding mercy in his heart for him, yet he does not send ṣalāh upon him.

The seventh reason: ṣalāh necessarily involves speech. It is praise from the one who sends ṣalāh upon the one for whom it is sent, and an honouring of him, extolling his virtues, what is in him, and mentioning him. Al-Bukhārī mentioned in his Ṣaḥīḥ from Abū al-ʿĀliyah who said: "The ṣalāh of God upon His Messenger is His praise of him in the presence of the angels." Ismāʿīl also said in his book: Naṣr ibn ʿAlī narrated to us, saying: Khālid ibn Yazīd narrated to us from Abū Jaʿfar from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas from Abū al-ʿĀliyah: "Indeed God and His angels send ṣalāh upon the Prophet." He said: "The ṣalāh of God, mighty and majestic, is His praise of him, and the ṣalāh of the angels upon him is supplication."

The eighth reason: God distinguished between His ṣalāh and the ṣalāh of His angels, yet combined them in a single act, saying: ﴿Indeed God and His angels send ṣalāh upon the Prophet﴾. This ṣalāh cannot be mercy. It is rather His praise and the praise of His angels for him.

It may not be said: ṣalāh is a homonymous term (lafẓ mushtarak), and it is permissible to use it in both of its meanings together.

For this would entail several serious problems.

The first: homonymy is contrary to the basic principle. It is not even known to have occurred in language from a single originator, as the imams of language, including al-Mubarrad and others, have stated. It occurs only accidentally, by chance, due to the plurality of those who coin words. Then language becomes mixed and homonymy arises.

The second: most scholars do not permit using a homonymous term in both of its meanings together, neither literally nor figuratively. What is reported from al-Shāfiʿī permitting this is not authentically from him. It arose from his saying: if he bequeaths to his *mawālī* (clients/masters), and he has *mawālī* above him and below him, they all are included. Some people thought that the word *mawlā* is homonymous between these two, and that when used without qualification it is understood as both. This is not correct. The word *mawlā* is a univocal term, and al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad in the apparent position of his school said that both types of *mawālī* enter into this term. For him it is a general univocal term, not a homonym.

As for what is reported from al-Shāfiʿī that he said, in a discussion that took place concerning God's words ﴿or you have touched women﴾, when it was said to him that *mulāmasah* may be intended as sexual intercourse, he said: it is understood literally as touching with the hand and figuratively as intercourse. This is not authentically from al-Shāfiʿī, nor is it of the kind of his familiar speech. Rather it comes from some later jurists. We have adduced in refutation of using a homonymous term in both its meanings together some fifteen proofs in the question of *qurʾ* (menstrual cycle/purity) in the book *al-Taʿlīq ʿalā al-Aḥkām*.

Therefore, if the meaning of ṣalāh is praise of the Messenger, care for him, and displaying his nobility, excellence and sanctity, as is well known from this word, then ṣalāh in the verse is not a homonym to be understood in both its meanings, but is used in one meaning. This is the basic principle in words. God willing, we will return to this question when discussing God's words: ﴿Indeed God and His angels send ṣalāh upon the Prophet﴾.

(Section)

Whoever wishes his structure to rise high must secure its foundation, make it firm, and give it the utmost care. For the height of a building is in proportion to the soundness and firmness of its foundation. Deeds and ranks are a building, and its foundation is faith (iman). When the foundation is sound, it bears the building and the building rises upon it; and if some part of the building collapses, it is easy to repair. But if the foundation is not sound, the building does not rise and does not stand; and if some part of the foundation collapses, the building falls or nearly falls. The one who has true knowledge (al-arif) directs his resolve to correcting the foundation and making it firm, while the ignorant one raises a structure without a foundation, so his building does not last long before it collapses. God Most High says: ﴿Is he who founded his building upon piety from God and His good pleasure better, or he who founded his building upon the brink of a crumbling, collapsing cliff, so that it collapsed with him into the fire of Hell?﴾

So the foundation for the building of deeds is like the strength of the human body. When the strength is great, it carries the body and repels many afflictions from it; when the strength is weak, its ability to carry the body weakens, and afflictions reach it most swiftly.

So carry your building upon the strength of the foundation of faith. Then, if some part of the upper structure and its surface becomes disordered, its repair is easier for you than the ruin of the foundation. This foundation consists of two matters: the soundness of knowledge of God, His commands, His names and His attributes; and the second is the singling out of submission to Him and to His Messenger, to the exclusion of anything else. This is the most secure foundation upon which the servant can establish his building, and in proportion to it the building may rise as high as it wills. So make the foundation firm, preserve the strength, persist in the regimen (al-himya), and purge when the corruptions increase within you. Moderation, moderation: you have then attained the aim. Otherwise, as long as the strength is weak and the corrupt matter is present and purging is absent...

﻿

(He says:)
"So convey the greeting to life, for it has already announced to you the swiftness of farewell."

When the building is complete, whiten it with good character and kindness to people. Then surround it with a wall of caution that no enemy can breach and from which no nakedness is exposed. Then let down curtains over its doors. Then lock the great door by keeping silent about what you fear its consequences. Then fashion for it a key of the remembrance of God, by which you open it and close it. If you open it, you open it with the key, and if you close the door, you close it with it. Then you will have built a fortress in which you are fortified against your enemies. When the enemy circles it, he finds no entrance into it, so he despairs of you. Then continually maintain the fortress's building at all times, for when the enemy does not hope to enter through the door, he digs breaches against you from afar with the pickaxes of sins. If you neglect his affair, the breach reaches you, and then the enemy is with you inside the fortress, and it becomes difficult for you to expel him, and you are with him in one of three states: either he overcomes you in the fortress and takes control of it, or he dwells alongside you in it, or he occupies you with confronting him away from the completion of your welfare, and you return to sealing the breach and repairing the fortress's damage. When he enters through his breach to you, three calamities befall you from him: corruption of the fortress, raiding its stores and treasures, and guiding the thieves of his own kind to its weak point. He keeps afflicting you with raids until they weaken your strength and enfeeble your resolve, so you abandon the fortress and leave it between them and him.

This is the condition of most souls with this enemy. Therefore you see them anger their Lord in pursuit of their own satisfaction, indeed in pursuit of the satisfaction of a created being like themselves who possesses no power to harm or benefit them. They squander the gain of religion for the gain of wealth, they destroy themselves for what will not remain for them, they covet the world while it has turned its back on them, they renounce the Hereafter while it has bore down upon them, they oppose their Lord by following their desires, they rely upon life and do not remember death, they remember their appetites and their portions and forget what God has entrusted to them, they concern themselves with what God has guaranteed and do not concern themselves with what He has commanded them, they rejoice in the world and grieve over the loss of their share of it, and do not grieve over the loss of Paradise and what is in it, and they do not rejoice in faith, their joy being in the dirham and the dinar. They corrupt their right and their guidance by their misguidance, their good by their wrongdoing, they clothe their faith with their suspicions, they mix their lawful with their unlawful, they wander in the bewilderment of their opinions and thoughts, and they abandon the guidance of God which He sent down to them. And the strange thing is that this enemy makes the owner of the fortress demolish his own fortress with his own hands.

(Section)

Sincere and accepted repentance has signs.

Among them: that after repentance one becomes better than one was before it.

Among them: that fear never leaves him; he does not feel safe from the scheming of Allah even for the blink of an eye. His fear continues until he hears the words of the messengers at the taking of his soul: ﴿Fear not, nor grieve, but rejoice in the Paradise which you were promised﴾ [Fussilat: 30]. At that point the fear departs.

Among them: that his heart is torn apart and shattered by remorse and fear, and this is in proportion to the greatness or smallness of the sin. This is Ibn 'Uyaynah's interpretation of the words of the Most High: ﴿Their building which they have built will not cease to be a cause of doubt in their hearts, unless their hearts are cut into pieces﴾ [al-Tawbah: 110].

He said: "Their hearts being cut into pieces" refers to repentance. There is no doubt that intense fear of a great punishment necessitates the splitting and tearing apart of the heart, and this is its being cut into pieces, and this is the reality of repentance. For his heart is torn apart by grief over what he has neglected and by fear of its evil consequence. Whoever does not have his heart torn apart in this world by grief and fear over what he neglected, will have it torn apart in the Hereafter when realities are made manifest, when he witnesses the reward of the obedient and the punishment of the disobedient. So there must be a tearing of the heart, either in this world or in the Hereafter.

Among the requirements of sincere repentance also: a particular brokenness that takes hold of the heart, resembling nothing else and not found in anyone other than the sinner. It is not attained through hunger, spiritual discipline, or mere love. Rather, it is something beyond all of this: it breaks the heart before its Lord with complete brokenness, encompassing it from every direction, and casts it before its Lord prostrate, humble and submissive, like the state of a sinful slave who has fled from his master, was seized and brought before him, found no one who could rescue him from his power, found no escape from him and no refuge from him, and knew that his life, happiness, success and triumph lie in his master's pleasure with him, knowing that his master is aware of every detail of his offenses, while also loving his master, being in dire need of him, knowing his own weakness and helplessness and his master's strength, his own lowliness and his master's might.

From these states there gathers brokenness, humiliation and submission: how beneficial it is for the servant, how fruitful its return to him! How great is his being mended through it, and how near he becomes to his master through it! Nothing is more beloved to his master than this brokenness, submission, humbling, lowliness, and prostration before Him, and surrender to Him. How sweet, by Allah, are his words in this state: "I ask You by Your might and my lowliness, that You have mercy on me. I ask You by Your strength and my weakness, and by Your independence from me and my need of You. Here is my forelock, lying and sinful, before You.
